title: Luqman's advice to his son
hookLine: Luqman the wise tells his son: don't associate anything with Allah (31:13)

lines: A FATHER TALKS TO HIS SON.
cards: Some advice from a parent arrives at a big moment: leaving home, a wedding, a hospital bed. Some arrives over the washing up, and only years later turns out to have stuck.
Surah Luqman, the thirty-first, is named for a man the Qur'an calls wise, and at its heart is a father talking to his son, piece by piece. The Qur'an keeps his words and lets us listen in.

teach.h: WHO WAS LUQMAN? THE QUR'AN IS QUIET.
teach.b: Who was Luqman? The Qur'an says only that God gave him wisdom, hikma, and that wisdom first meant: give thanks to God. Beyond that, the sources are quiet.
Later tradition says he was from Africa, perhaps Nubia or Abyssinia, and reports differ on whether he was a tailor, a carpenter or a shepherd.
Scholars have asked whether he was a prophet; tradition mostly remembers him as a wise man, and the Qur'an doesn't settle it. What it gives is his words.
Pickthall: "O my dear son! Ascribe no partners unto Allah. Lo! to ascribe partners (unto Him) is a tremendous wrong."
Start with ya bunayya: not just ibni, my son, but the small, tender form, my dear boy. The weightiest advice starts with affection.
Ascribing partners is shirk: treating anything else, money, power, a person, an idol, as if it shared God's place. Luqman calls it zulm 'azim, a tremendous wrong.
The classical dictionaries define zulm as putting something where it doesn't belong. A hadith in Bukhari shows how much this verse mattered.
When another verse said safety belongs to those who don't mix their faith with zulm, the companions were frightened: which of us hasn't wronged himself?
The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told them it doesn't mean that; it means what Luqman told his son: shirk is a tremendous wrong.
So the first advice puts first things first. Before manners, prayer, or how to walk and talk, which come later in the speech: know who God is, and put nothing in His place.

how: Muslim parents and teachers often use Luqman's advice in 31:13–19 as a model for raising children, beginning with tawhid, the oneness of God.

o: a judge famed for settling family quarrels
the scribe who first wrote down the Qur'an
a wise man whose advice to his son the Qur'an keeps

p: my dear son, the tender form
putting something where it doesn't belong

s: the Qur'an says Luqman was a prophet
it says he was given wisdom, and leaves the question open.
Luqman's first advice is about manners
it's about God: ascribe no partners to Him.
Luqman calls his son by a tender, diminutive form
ya bunayya: my dear son, my little boy.

games.q: the companions hear that safety is for those who don't mix faith with wrong. they panic: who hasn't wronged himself? what does the Prophet say?
o: it means shirk, as Luqman told his son.
games.why: a hadith in Bukhari: he pointed them to Luqman's words, that shirk is a tremendous wrong.

practice: Think of the best advice anyone ever gave you, the one that actually changed something, and remember who gave it and how; was there tenderness in it?
Then think of someone younger or newer who might need it someday, and hear how you'd say it, starting the way Luqman did, with affection. If you pray, you can pray for that person by name.

wordCard.voice: Luqman. The wise man of surah thirty-one, whose speech to his son starts, my dear son, and puts first: don't ascribe partners to God. Today's word.
